decision_clues.source_quote: The proposed design consists of a cascaded dielectric multilayer architecture combining SiOF, Si3N4, and BaSnO3 to achieve high visible-light transmittance together with broadband NIR rejection.
decision_clues.structure_or_method: Cascaded dielectric multilayer architecture for spectral separation.
decision_clues.physical_effect: Broadband NIR rejection while preserving daylight transmission via photonic band gap engineering.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source targets visible transmission/NIR rejection; task requires UV transmission/visible-NIR rejection.
Materials (SiOF, Si3N4, BaSnO3) differ from the execution inventory (MgF2, Al2O3, etc.).
No numerical data for 255-280 nm range provided.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Hypothesize that a similar cascaded stack topology, adapted to UV-transparent materials (MgF2/Al2O3), can create a short-wave pass characteristic allowing UV while blocking longer wavelengths.

decision_clues.source_quote: Reflective multilayer coatings based on two dielectrics have higher peak performance but lower out-ofband rejection than Al/MgF 2 transmittance filters. The main material combinations are (MgF 2 or AlF 3 )/(LaF 3 or GdF 3 ).
decision_clues.structure_or_method: All-dielectric reflective multilayers using fluoride pairs.
decision_clues.physical_effect: High peak reflectance/transmittance in UV; trade-off in out-of-band rejection width.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source discusses reflective mirrors or Al-based filters; task requires all-dielectric transmission filters.
LaF3/GdF3 are not in the execution inventory; MgF2 is available.
Specific layer counts for broad stopbands not detailed.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Transfer the principle of using low-absorption fluorides (MgF2) paired with a higher-index stable oxide (Al2O3/HfO2) to construct a bandpass filter, accepting that wider stopbands may require more layers or specific stacking sequences.

decision_clues.source_quote: By tuning the optical thickness such that UV wavelengths (300-400 nm) fall near destructive-interference condi-tions, the coating effectively suppresses UV transmission [7]. In contrast, longer visible wavelengths lie closer to constructive interference, which preserves high transmittance in the 400-700 nm range.
decision_clues.structure_or_method: Optical thickness tuning for wavelength-selective interference.
decision_clues.physical_effect: Destructive interference for suppression bands, constructive for passbands.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source describes UV blocking/Visible passing; task is the inverse (UV passing/Visible blocking).
Wavelength ranges differ (source 300-400 nm vs task 255-280 nm pass).
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Reverse the design logic: tune optical thickness so that 255-280 nm experiences constructive interference (high transmission) while 300-1100 nm experiences destructive interference (low transmission).

decision_clues.source_quote: The practical bandpass filter is composed of periodic SiO2/Si bilayers alternatively deposited layer-by-layer on the backside of a thermal oxidized Si substrate... The filter is composed of 32 layers, providing a total thickness of 6.02 m.
decision_clues.structure_or_method: Periodic bilayer stacks for bandpass filtering.
decision_clues.physical_effect: Interference effect creating a passband with wide stopband coverage.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source uses Si/SiO2 (absorbing high-index) which is unsuitable for UV transmission.
Target wavelength (1550 nm) differs significantly from UV.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Adapt the periodic bilayer concept using transparent UV materials (MgF2/Nb2O5) and optimize layer count to fit within 30 layers while targeting the UV passband.

decision_clues.source_quote: To achieve an arbitrary BW, the refractive indices of the coating materials must be changed... assume that the high-index material is Nb 2 O 5 with n H = 2.25... and the low-index material is SiO 2 with n L = 1.45
decision_clues.structure_or_method: Refractive index contrast manipulation for bandwidth control.
decision_clues.physical_effect: Higher index contrast enables broader stopbands or narrower passbands depending on design.
conditions_and_unknowns: Source targets 1550 nm; UV indices and dispersion will differ.
SiO2 absorption edge may be relevant below 200nm, but likely acceptable at 255nm.
Nb2O5 is in the execution inventory.
decision_clues.inference_bridge: Utilize the high index contrast between Nb2O5 (or HfO2/Ta2O5) and MgF2/SiO2 to maximize the stopband width covering 300-1100 nm with fewer layers.

routes.claim: A symmetric Fabry-Perot cavity using MgF2 spacers and Nb2O5 mirrors can isolate the 255-280 nm band, leveraging high index contrast to widen the rejection bands towards visible and NIR.
transfer_assumptions: Nb2O5 and MgF2 maintain sufficient transparency and index contrast at 255 nm despite source data being at visible/NIR wavelengths.
A single-cavity design can provide adequate rejection across the broad 300-1100 nm range without exceeding 30 layers.

expectations.controlled_conditions: Same stack symmetry, materials, and substrate.
expectations.reason: Baseline is tuned for peak; candidate adjusts mirror thicknesses primarily to affect stopband width, potentially slightly shifting but maintaining high UV transmission.

expectations.controlled_conditions: Same stack symmetry, materials, and substrate.
expectations.reason: Increasing index contrast effect via optimized quarter-wave matching in mirrors should deepen/widen the rejection band.

routes.model_knowledge_rationale: Standard thin-film theory suggests that increasing the number of periods in the Bragg mirrors surrounding the cavity deepens the stopband. The specific thickness values are estimated based on quarter-wave optical thickness at the center of the UV passband (~267 nm), adjusted for the available material indices.

routes.claim: A multi-cavity design using Ta2O5 and SiO2 can sharpen the passband edges, improving rejection in the adjacent visible band (300-400 nm) while maintaining UV transmission.
transfer_assumptions: Ta2O5 is sufficiently transparent at 255 nm (some absorption may occur near 250 nm, requiring verification).
Multi-cavity coupling can be achieved within the 30-layer limit.

expectations.controlled_conditions: Same material order and layer count.
expectations.reason: Coupling cavities can flatten the passband top, potentially increasing the integrated mean transmission over the 25 nm band.

expectations.controlled_conditions: Same material order and layer count.
expectations.reason: Multi-cavity designs typically exhibit steeper skirts, reducing transmission in the immediate adjacent visible band.

open_requirements: Verify Ta2O5 absorption coefficient at 255 nm in the local dataset before execution.

routes.claim: A 'rugate-like' discrete approximation using varying thicknesses of Al2O3 and MgF2 can suppress side-lobes in the visible region, improving rejection uniformity.
transfer_assumptions: Discrete layer steps can approximate a graded index profile sufficiently to reduce sidelobes.
Al2O3 is transparent enough at 255 nm.

expectations.reason: Apodization (varying layer thicknesses) is theoretically expected to reduce sidelobe levels in the stopband compared to a uniform periodic stack.

routes.model_knowledge_rationale: Rugate filters theoretically eliminate sidelobes by continuous index variation. In discrete multilayers, stepping the optical thicknesses (apodization) mimics this effect. Al2O3 is chosen for its robustness and moderate index.

routes.claim: Exploiting the dispersion of MgF2 and Nb2O5, a non-quarter-wave stack optimized specifically for 255-280 nm transmission can achieve broader NIR rejection than a standard quarter-wave design centered at the same wavelength.
transfer_assumptions: Numerical optimization of non-standard thicknesses can leverage material dispersion to widen the stopband.
Dispersion data in the execution inventory is accurate for the UV range.

expectations.reason: Non-quarter-wave thicknesses can shift higher-order harmonics or broaden the fundamental stopband through constructive interference of reflections at different wavelengths.

routes.claim: A detuned stack where layer thicknesses gradually increase from the substrate to the incident medium can compensate for field distribution asymmetry, potentially improving damage threshold or transmission uniformity.
transfer_assumptions: Field distribution in the UV passband is asymmetric due to substrate index mismatch.
Thickness grading can mitigate standing wave peaks.

expectations.reason: Grading may better match the impedance profile, reducing ripple in the passband.

routes.model_knowledge_rationale: Impedance matching concepts from microwave engineering applied to optics suggest that graded index profiles reduce reflections. In discrete layers, stepping the thicknesses approximates this gradient.
